_note: Per-language data read by scripts/speech_split.py and scripts/language_checks.py. One source of truth: the /translate-prompt skill and its reference/plain-speech.md point here instead of repeating it. Every entry outside Hindi is a SEED written by the tuner, not by a native speaker: review="needs-native" means a named speaker must confirm it before the language is called verified. 'formal' maps a bookish word to the word people actually say on the phone (a hit is a WARNING with the suggestion, never an automatic edit). 'denylist' holds the common insulting words for disabilities: the bot must never say them, and they belong in the agent's speech-recognition vocabulary so callers who use them are understood. 'min_terms' is the minimum coverage every language's everyday-word table must have (from the Purple Dots language-testing sheet).

hi.name: Hindi
hi.gender: Verbs mark gender in the first, second and third person, in the past, progressive and future (करती हूँ / करता हूँ; आप आए / आईं). The bot's own lines use its voice gender everywhere. Lines to the caller use the respectful plural (आप ... करते हैं / रहे हैं), which is the accepted neutral form, until the caller's gender is known.
hi.question: क्या at the start or a rising final particle, written with ?

mr.name: Marathi
mr.gender: First-person verbs mark the speaker's gender (करते / करतो, बोलते / बोलतो): the bot uses its voice gender. Lines to the caller use तुम्ही with plural verbs (तुम्ही आलात, तुम्ही सांगाल), which do not reveal the caller's gender. Third-person past marks gender (तो आला / ती आली): use the child's or caller's own word, or a plural, until it is known.
mr.question: the particle का at the end (आहे का?) or a question word, written with ?

kn.name: Kannada
kn.gender: First- and second-person verbs carry no gender (ನಾನು ಮಾಡ್ತೀನಿ, ನೀವು ಮಾಡ್ತೀರಾ). Only the third person singular marks it (ಅವನು ಬಂದ / ಅವಳು ಬಂದಳು): use ಅವರು (respectful plural) for any third person whose gender is unknown. A Hindi example that teaches masculine vs feminine verb forms has no Kannada equivalent: replace it with the ಅವರು rule, do not translate it into two identical lines.
kn.question: the suffix -ಆ on the verb (ಇದೆಯಾ? ಬೇಕಾ?) or a question word, written with ?

te.name: Telugu
te.gender: First- and second-person verbs carry no gender (నేను చేస్తాను, మీరు చేస్తారు). The third person singular separates masculine from everything else (అతను వచ్చాడు / ఆమె వచ్చింది): use the respectful plural (వారు / ఆయన-ఆవిడ only once known). Never translate a Hindi gendered-verb example into two identical lines.
te.question: the suffix -ఆ (ఉందా? కావాలా?) or a question word, written with ?

or.name: Odia
or.gender: Odia verbs carry no grammatical gender in any person. Do not invent a gender rule; replace any Hindi gendered-verb example with a one-line note that Odia has none.
or.question: the particle କି (ଅଛି କି?) or a question word, written with ?. Odia shares the Hindi sentence-ending mark (।): it is NOT Hindi residue.

as.name: Assamese
as.script: Assamese (Bengali script with ৰ and ৱ)
as.gender: Assamese verbs carry no grammatical gender in any person. Replace any Hindi gendered-verb example with a one-line note that Assamese has none.
as.question: the particle নে / নেকি (আছে নে?) or a question word, written with ?. Assamese shares the sentence-ending mark (।) with Hindi: it is NOT Hindi residue.

ta.name: Tamil
ta.gender: First- and second-person verbs carry no gender; the third person singular marks masculine vs feminine (அவன் / அவள்): use the respectful அவங்க / அவர் until known.
ta.question: the suffix -ஆ (இருக்கா?) or a question word, written with ?

ml.name: Malayalam
ml.gender: Malayalam verbs do not change for person or gender at all.
ml.question: the suffix -ഓ (ഉണ്ടോ?), written with ?

bn.name: Bengali
bn.gender: Bengali verbs carry no grammatical gender.
bn.question: কি / কী or a question word, written with ?

gu.name: Gujarati
gu.gender: Past and perfect verbs and many adjectives mark three genders; follow the Hindi approach (respectful plural to the caller).
gu.question: શું or a final ને, written with ?

pa.name: Punjabi
pa.gender: Like Hindi: verbs mark gender in most tenses; use the respectful plural to the caller.
pa.question: ਕੀ at the start, written with ?

ur.name: Urdu
ur.gender: Like Hindi: verbs mark gender in most tenses; use the respectful plural to the caller.
ur.question: کیا at the start, written with ؟
